picked.t: Mother-in-law bridges cultural gap for Vietnamese bride marrying into a Malaysian Muslim family
picked.body: Even Vi’s parents had feared that the geographical distance as well as cultural and religious differences could cause conflicts in married life. At one point, her mother suggested that Vi should return to Vietnam to rethink things. Vi's father simply said: "I trust your decision." While Vi's family was still filled with hesitation, Amirrashid’s mother took the initiative to help both sides understand each other. Having lived in Australia for many years, she had an open-minded view of cultural and religious differences. She told her son and Vi that while religion is important, the couple's life together after marriage is equally crucial. Knowing that Vi’s parents were worried, she video-called them to ask for their approval of the couple’s marriage. She said Vi would not have to convert to Islam or change her lifestyle just to marry her son. "She said as long as the two of them live happily and joyfully, that's all that matters," Vi says. After the conversation, her parents were gradually reassured. The openness of Amirrashid’s family also gave her greater confidence about marrying a foreigner from a different religious background. The two had met in Australia. Amirrashid had emigrated to the country with his mother in 2017, while Vi went in 2022 on a working holiday visa. She worked at a fruit packing warehouse, where he was a supervisor. The two lived close to each other, and so she would ask him to take her to work every day since there were no buses and a rideshare cost around VND200,000 (US$7.7) one way. He refused to take money from her though she shyly offered several times to pay him. To thank him, she invited him out for a meal. After the meal, Amirrashid drove Vi around the city. They chatted about work, life, and future plans. From those rides to work and after-work meals, the two gradually realized they had much in common. Three months later, they officially started dating. Her initial impression of Amirrashid was that he was cold and unapproachable, but the more time she spent with him, the more she realized that behind that exterior was an honest, warm-hearted man who respected others' decisions and cherished his family. Every time she made a video call to her family in Vietnam, he would learn a few simple Vietnamese phrases to greet her parents. But when marriage loomed, they had to confront the question of how to coexist across two different cultures. She researched potential cultural clashes in family life, and clearly told him that she still wanted to study, work, and pursue her passions after marriage. He agreed. The couple also discussed family principles related to Amirul's religion beforehand, rather than waiting until they lived together to start adapting. Following their engagement ceremony in Australia in 2025, which some 30 people attended, the couple decided to hold their wedding in Vietnam in July according to her family traditions. Around 50 of his relatives and friends traveled from Malaysia to attend the wedding. Vi’s family invited around 300 guests and had six separate banquet tables for the groom's family with chicken and seafood that complied with his family’s dietary restrictions. On wedding day, the bride and groom wore traditional Malaysian attire to welcome guests, and then changed into a suit and wedding gown for the ceremony on stage. Finally, they wore the Vietnamese attire, ao dai, to greet every guest table. Despite the language barrier, relatives from both sides found ways to chat and blend into the atmosphere. They danced and sang together; even Amirrashid’s maternal grandmother was present to witness the couple's special day. "Our wedding was very lively. Both families danced and sang together; despite the language barrier, we were still in harmony. That is what made me feel the happiest," Vy says. After the wedding, the couple have moved to Australia. Vi gradually realized that her mother-in-law's promise manifested in the small details of everyday life: She does not have to change her way of dressing or wear a headscarf when going outside. Amirrashid does not ask his wife to give up her studies or career. The couple shares household chores: one cooks while the other washes the dishes, one does the laundry while the other mops the floors. Before getting married, they mostly ate out because neither knew how to cook. After moving in together, they learned how to make food that suits them both. Amirul does not eat pork for religious reasons, and so family meals usually consist of chicken and fish. Vi never liked pork to begin with, and so does not find this inconvenient. For her, the biggest change after marriage is not adapting to a new religion; it is learning how two people with differences can live together in harmony. "I am happy to have found my husband. I think cultural and language differences are not a big deal when both know how to love and look out for each other."

picked.t: Driving from Hanoi to Paris: 68 days through 20 countries
picked.body: On July 6, the group led by Do Minh Ho Hai set off from Hanoi. "The goal was not to arrive as quickly as possible, but to enjoy the scenery and explore the culture and daily life of the places between the start and the end," Hai says. Each vehicle carried one or two members. The group traveled in seven cars and two motorbikes, and passed through 20 countries including China, Turkey, and Germany. While returning, they chose to fly. This was not a typical road trip. Hai calls it a rally-style journey. The vehicles shared the same route and destination, but each traveled at its own speed and chose rest stops, and did not travel in a convoy. After every two to three days of driving, the group took a day off to explore the city they had just reached. The members spent a year preparing. They trained physically, secured all travel documents, and mapped out their route. They also came up with plans in case a vehicle or a member ran into trouble. "For us, the year of preparation was just as important as the 68 days on the road," Hai says. All the vehicles were SUVs or pickup trucks fitted with all-terrain tires, and could handle highways, rocky roads, and areas far from cities. China was where the group stayed the longest, 17 days. But for Hai, the longest day of the trip came when they left China to enter Kyrgyzstan. The group spent 13 hours at the border, checking documents and processing paperwork for 16 people and their vehicles. It was 2 a.m. before everyone reached the hotel, exhausted. Hai says the main worry was not the wait but that a problem with the papers of just one member or one vehicle could have meant the whole group would have to change plans. Fortunately, everyone crossed over safely. But Kyrgyzstan was also the country that overwhelmed him most with its scenery. In 2025, after watching the Netflix film "Off Road", he was captivated by the Altyn-Arashan Valley. Situated at a height of over 2,300 meters, the valley has meadows, pine forests, glaciers, and hot springs. He had told himself that one day he would drive a Vietnamese-plated car there. On July 27, that wish came true. The 14-kilometer Altyn-Arashan road took two hours to navigate due to its steep slopes and cliffside bends. A single mistake could send the car over the edge. Over 68 days, chance encounters with locals became the memories Hai kept longest. In Chechnya, they met a melon farmer. Learning that the group had driven all the way from Vietnam, he sliced melons for everyone, refused payment and asked only for a photo. "Some encounters lasted only a few minutes, but I remember them long after the journey," Hai says. Another memorable moment came when Russian police fined some of the vehicles $150. Window tint is illegal in Russia and many Central Asian countries, risking fines and removal if pulled over. The trip cost about VND600 million (US$23,080) per person, including VND300 million for food, hotels and tours. Each car cost up to VND400 million for fuel, tolls and maintenance, plus up to VND200 million for return shipping to Vietnam. Several companies sponsored the tires. In Europe, roads were easier to travel but prices were higher. Parking could cost up to 50 euros ($57) a day, and fuel about VND75,000 ($2.90) per liter. "Every trip to a gas station was like getting pickpocketed," Hai jokes. In the Czech Republic, travel enthusiasts came to the hotel to film Hai's group. He also had a chance to try what he called Europe's best tiet canh , or raw blood pudding, at a Vietnamese restaurant. After 65 days on the road, five of the nine cars reached Paris on Sept. 8, bringing Hai a sense of relief. The group spent another three days exploring the city before flying home. The other cars took different routes through Europe before joining them in Paris. Over dinner that evening, the discussion shifted from planning the next day's route to sharing memories of the journey. Nguyen Phuong Nga, one of two women in the group, was shocked at the thought of a 68-day trip. She still decided to join her husband. Besides gifts for her family, her luggage on the way home included about 2 kilograms of fridge magnets. On Sept. 13, Hai landed in Ho Chi Minh City, ending a journey of 22,000 kilometers. After each trip, he finds that he sees things more simply, and that the world holds many places worth visiting at least once in a lifetime. In 2027, Hai plans to drive from Hanoi to Moscow. But for now, one "procedure" he considers the most important has yet to be completed: "Waiting for my wife's approval!"

picked.t: Vietnam's latest coffee experiment comes with fermented shrimp paste
picked.body: Since early September, TOC Gallery at 4 Nguyen Thi Minh Khai Street, Thuan Hoa Ward, Hue City, has seen a 20% rise in customers after introducing a shrimp paste coffee. The beverage is now its signature item, selling about 50 cups a day at VND55,000 (US$2.10) each. Tran Ngoc Anh Tuan, 32, the cafe's co-owner, came up with the idea after wanting to infuse the character of Hue's cuisine into a drink. Hue was already famous for its salt coffee. So when developing something new, he and his team wanted to stand out while keeping the local soul. They chose to experiment with mam ruoc , which is central to Hue cuisine. Mam ruoc is made by mixing ruoc or sea shrimp with salt and leaving it to ferment in clay jars. The condiment shapes the flavor of many local dishes, including bun bo Hue (spicy beef noodle soup) and com hen (baby clam rice). Tuan says its saltiness pairs well with coffee. A sour ingredient would spoil the creamy layer on top, he explains. " Ruoc is a familiar seasoning in Hue kitchens, but it has never been used in drinks." Many people dismissed the idea as absurd, but the team pressed on and perfected the recipe after six months. The shrimp paste is cooked with caramel sugar and cream to mitigate its odor and infuse a light aroma. Each cup has four layers of flavor. At the bottom is milk blended with condensed milk, followed by coffee made from a mixture of Arabica beans grown in A Luoi, a mountainous area of Hue, and robusta. The top is a shrimp paste cream, finished with shavings of dried tuna. To taste each layer, Tuan advises drinkers to skip the straw. Instead, they should stir the coffee and milk below, leaving the shrimp paste cream untouched. Sipping straight from the rim lets the cream mingle with the bitterness of the coffee, leaving a fragrant aftertaste. The name alone makes many customers curious, and, admittedly, many hesitant, when they first hear it. Quoc Bao, 28, of Ho Chi Minh City says he was surprised that the smell of the paste was not as strong as he had imagined. The coffee remained the dominant flavor, with the saltiness lingering in the aftertaste. To Bao, it is a drink "worth trying" when visiting Hue. Bich Ngoc, 35, a tourist from Nghe An Province, sought out the drink after seeing many people share it on social media. "I was a bit wary at first because I never thought shrimp paste could go with coffee, but after trying it, I found it quite interesting," she says.
